angle: The 3 buckets of signals: out-of-the-box, custom, and first-party
post_first_line: 3 buckets cover every signal we use.
linkedin_post:
3 buckets cover every signal we use.

Cole Courson says there could be more, but simplifying into three makes the whole thing usable.

Bucket one is out-of-the-box signals. These are things providers like Unify, Clay, and Sixsense give you with a flip of a switch: website intent tracking, persona-level tracking, champion tracking, new hires, and job changes.

Cole's take is that these are interesting at layer one, but they get more interesting when compounded with other signals.

Bucket two is custom signals. Think technographics, job scraping for hiring in specific roles, and social listening on Reddit, GitHub, or Glassdoor to find pain.

Cole called these really, really important to dive into.

The out-of-the-box layer gets everyone started. The custom layer is where a team starts to build something nobody else has.

Which bucket is your team leaning on most?

Slide 2: Bucket one: out-of-the-box signals you flip on.
Slide 3: Website intent, persona tracking, champion tracking, new hires, job changes.
Slide 4: Interesting alone, but more powerful when compounded.
Slide 5: Bucket two: custom signals built around your market.
Slide 6: Technographics, job scraping, and hiring for specific roles.
Slide 7: Social listening on Reddit, GitHub, and Glassdoor surfaces pain.
Slide 8: Simplify to buckets so your team can actually act.

lesson.title: Organizing signals into simple buckets
takeaways: Out-of-the-box signals like intent, champion tracking, new hires, and job changes are quick to turn on and interesting at layer one.
Custom signals like technographics, job scraping, and social listening on Reddit, GitHub, or Glassdoor are worth diving into.
Signals get more interesting when you compound them rather than use them alone.
lesson.exercise: List every signal your team tracks today and sort each into out-of-the-box or custom. Then pick one custom signal, like hiring for a specific role, to pair with an out-of-the-box one.

angle: Two things Google flags in high-volume cold email, and how to avoid them
linkedin_post:
Cole Courson sends 200k+ emails monthly.

Google flags two things at that volume, and most senders miss the second one.

The first is sameness. When every email looks identical to the next, filters notice. Cole's fix is small, deliberate variability in each message.

That means dynamic snippets: first name, last name, company name, sender name, and spintax.

None of these changes the offer. Together they make each email a little different from the one before it, which helps at large scale.

The second is a subject line that disconnects from the body. If the subject says one thing and the message says another, Google treats it as spam.

So the subject line has to match what the email actually talks about.

Broad, high-volume campaigns don't need to look like blasts. They need variation and a subject line that tells the truth.

What's your go-to snippet for adding variability?
carousel: Slide 1: Sending 200 to 400k cold emails a month?
Slide 2: Google flags two things at that volume.
Slide 3: Flag one: every email looks like the last one.
Slide 4: Add variability with first name, last name, and company.
Slide 5: Add the sender name and spintax snippets too.
Slide 6: Flag two: the subject line disconnects from the body.
Slide 7: A subject that doesn't match the message reads as spam.
Slide 8: Vary each email and keep subject and body aligned.

lesson.title: Two things Google flags in high-volume cold email
takeaways: Low variability from one email to the next gets flagged, so use dynamic snippets like first name, last name, company name, sender name, and spintax.
Small variations add up and help broad campaigns land at large scale.
A subject line that disconnects from the body of the message gets flagged as spam.
lesson.exercise: Open your highest-volume campaign and add at least three dynamic snippets, such as first name, company name, and sender name. Then read each subject line next to its body and rewrite any that don't match.

angle: Why one big send day can get your mailboxes cancelled and cost you a month of warmup
post_first_line: 100,000 emails after weeks of 50 a day?
linkedin_post:
100,000 emails after weeks of 50 a day?

That one decision can wipe out a month of work.

Cole Courson has seen what happens when sending volume jumps overnight. Google flags the break in pattern. Mailboxes get cancelled and domains get shut down.

Say a team sends 50 emails a day, every day. Then a webinar comes along and the list goes out in one blast. Every one of those messages gets flagged.

The damage doesn't stop at spam folders. Those messages disappear into the ether, and the domains need to be warmed up again. Warming up typically takes 2 to 3 weeks, so the recovery runs about a month.

Cole has been through it, and called it a really painful process.

Google watches for consistency. Steady volume looks normal, and a sudden spike looks like a problem.

Want to send more? Scale up gradually instead of in one jump.

What's the biggest send spike you've ever tried?
carousel: Slide 1: 50 emails a day, then 100,000 in one day.
Slide 2: Google flags sudden breaks in your daily send volume.
Slide 3: Flagged mailboxes get cancelled and domains get shut down.
Slide 4: Warming up domains typically takes 2 to 3 weeks.
Slide 5: One big blast can cost you a full month.
Slide 6: Messages sent during the spike vanish into the ether.
Slide 7: Cole Courson has been through it. Painful process.
Slide 8: Want bigger volume? Scale it out gradually.

lesson.title: Why Send Volume Consistency Protects Your Mailboxes
takeaways: Google flags sudden jumps from your normal daily send volume, such as going from 50 a day to 100,000.
Cancelled mailboxes and shut-down domains mean restarting warmup, which typically takes 2 to 3 weeks.
To send larger volumes, scale up gradually instead of in one big day.
lesson.exercise: Write down your current daily send volume per mailbox, then plan a step-by-step ramp for any upcoming campaign or webinar send instead of one big blast.

angle: 'Saw you on our website' is lazy: give prospects a real reason to talk to you
post_first_line: Bobby Foose rejects "saw you on our website."
linkedin_post:
Bobby Foose rejects "saw you on our website."

It's the most common cold opener, and it says the least.

Bobby's point: put yourself in the other person's shoes. Why would they want to talk to you? A very valid answer is that they don't.

So the job is to give them a reason that has nothing to do with the pitch.

"Saw you on our website" is lazy. It doesn't show any homework at all.

Compare that to something personal. Something like: "You're from Bobby's hometown. Bobby is out in San Francisco now, working at a startup called Unify."

That opener gives the reader a reason to keep reading before the pitch even starts.

The bar for a first message is not "relevant." It's "worth a reply from someone who owes you nothing."

What's the best opener you've ever received?
carousel: Slide 1: "Saw you on our website" is a lazy opener.
Slide 2: It tells the prospect you did zero homework.
Slide 3: Put yourself in their shoes: why would they talk to you?
Slide 4: A very valid answer is that they wouldn't.
Slide 5: So find a reason that goes beyond your website.
Slide 6: Try a real connection, like a shared hometown.
Slide 7: Then say who you are and what you do.
Slide 8: Earn the reply before you make the pitch.

lesson.title: Give prospects a real reason to talk to you
takeaways: "Saw you on our website" signals no homework and gives the prospect no reason to engage.
Assume the prospect has no desire to talk to you, then work to change that.
A genuine personal connection, like a shared hometown, earns attention before the pitch.
lesson.exercise: Rewrite your last three cold openers. Replace any "saw you on your website" line with one specific, personal connection to the prospect, then follow with one sentence on who you are and what you do.

caption: Stop saying "saw your website"

angle: Stop obsessing over Gmail vs Outlook: org size and a single channel are the bigger deliverability problem
post_first_line: Cole Courson: stop obsessing over Gmail vs Outlook.
linkedin_post:
Cole Courson: stop obsessing over Gmail vs Outlook.

The bigger deliverability problem sits somewhere else.

According to Cole, org size matters more. Emailing into large organizations is just tougher. They have spam checkers and blockers, and sometimes they pay for platforms that don't let your emails through.

Best practices are still best practices. Get those right first.

But after that, Cole would worry more about these nuances than about which inbox provider the buyer uses.

That's where multichannel comes in. Use signals and intent to send a good email, then refer to that email in a cold call so the rep gets a real opportunity.

Cole acknowledged it was an email course. The recommendation was still to use all channels, and there are 3 of them.

What channel do you lean on too heavily?
carousel: Slide 1: Gmail vs Outlook is not your real deliverability problem
Slide 2: Org size makes a bigger difference than inbox provider
Slide 3: Large orgs run spam checkers and blockers
Slide 4: Some pay for platforms that stop your emails entirely
Slide 5: Get the email best practices right first
Slide 6: Then stop relying on email alone
Slide 7: Use signals and intent to send a good email
Slide 8: Reference that email in a cold call to open the door

lesson.title: Deliverability Is Bigger Than Your Inbox Provider
takeaways: Emailing into large organizations is tougher because of spam checkers, blockers, and paid filtering platforms.
Best practices come first, but org size nuances deserve more worry than Gmail vs Outlook.
Multichannel helps: send a good email based on signals and intent, then reference it in a cold call.
lesson.exercise: List your target accounts by org size. For the largest ones, plan a follow-up cold call that references the email you sent.

angle: 300-400K emails a month run by one orchestrator, and why a case study like that belongs in your email framework
linkedin_post:
300-400K emails a month. One orchestrator.

That's the case study Cole Courson says belongs in your email framework before you write a single email.

Cole works with one POC at Guru, who sends roughly 300 to 400K emails a month. With one orchestrator and Cole running it, the whole thing stays clean.

The result: saved time, saved energy, and marketing results still moving. That becomes a story you can tell other prospects.

A typical email framework includes the question: what type of story have we helped them draw away from? A case study like this answers it.

Cole's point is that before email one of founder-led sales, you need to know where you want to start. That means the personas, the splits, the pains, and the stories.

The stories come first. The copy comes after.

What story would you lead your first email with?

Slide 8: Stories first. Copy second.

lesson.title: Pick your stories before you write email one
takeaways: An email framework should include the story of what you've helped others move away from.
A strong case study can be as simple as less time, less energy, and the same marketing results.
For founder-led sales, define personas, splits, pains, and stories before drafting email one.
lesson.exercise: Write down one customer result in a sentence: what they were doing before, what changed, and the outcome. Then map it to a persona and a pain you'd target in email one.
